Naamathite
NAY-uh-muh-thite
proper noun (gentilic)
Hebrew Naamathi (H5284), an inhabitant of Naamah, a place otherwise unknown; the root naem (H5276) means to be pleasant or agreeable.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs four times in Scripture and always of one man: Zophar the Naamathite, the third of Job's three friends. He came with Eliphaz and Bildad when they heard of all the evil that had come upon Job, for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him (Job 2:11), and they began well — seven days and seven nights on the ground beside him, and none spake a word. Then the speeches began. Zophar speaks twice (Job 11 and 20), and he is the harshest of the three: he tells Job that God exacts of him less than his iniquity deserves, and devotes a whole chapter to the short triumphing of the wicked. He does not speak a third time; the argument runs out. At the end the LORD's verdict falls on all three: ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath (Job 42:7), and they were commanded to bring a burnt offering and let Job pray for them — and the LORD also accepted Job (Job 42:9).

Origin & Era

An inhabitant of Naamah; in Scripture always the designation of Zophar, the third of Job's three friends.

NAAMATHITE, Hebrew Naamathi, an inhabitant of Naamah.

The standing description of Zophar, the third of the three friends of Job.

He came with Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite to mourn with Job and to comfort him.

He spake twice, in the eleventh and the twentieth chapters, and the harshest of the three.

The LORD rebuked all three and required a burnt offering, and Job prayed for them.

Key Scripture

Job 2:11 — "Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him."

Job 11:1 — "Then answered Zophar the Naamathite, and said,"

Job 20:1 — "Then answered Zophar the Naamathite, and said,"

Job 42:9 — "So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went, and did according as the LORD commanded them: the LORD also accepted Job."

Modern Corruption

Suffering is read as a reliable index of guilt; the book of Job exists to refute that reading, and God rebukes the men who made it.

expand to see more

Zophar's theology is not exotic. It is the ordinary retribution principle held rigidly: God is just, God governs, therefore the man in ashes has earned his ashes. It is the same reasoning the disciples brought to the blind man — who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind? — and the Lord Jesus answered Neither (Joh 9:2-3). He said the same about the Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices, and the eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell: they were not sinners above all others (Luk 13:1-5). The book of Job is in the canon largely to kill this inference, and it kills it by telling the reader in chapter one what none of the characters know.

The modern form of the error is the prosperity teaching in reverse: if a believer is sick, poor or crushed, some hidden fault must account for it — unconfessed sin, a lack of faith, a wrong confession. The counsel that follows is Zophar's counsel in a softer accent, and it does the same damage. The principle to recover is the one God vindicated: a man may be upright, may fear God and eschew evil, and may still be broken; and the friends who came to comfort him ended up needing him to pray for them. Sit on the ground for seven days if necessary, and be very slow to explain another man's affliction to him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Naamathi (H5284), from the place-name Naamah; the root naem (H5276) signifies pleasantness.

expand to see more

Hebrew Naamathi (H5284) — a Naamathite; Job 2:11, 11:1, 20:1, 42:9.

Hebrew naem (H5276) — to be pleasant, agreeable, delightful; the root behind Naomi and Naaman.

Hebrew Tsophar (H6691) — Zophar, the third friend; the name suggests chirping or a small bird.

Hebrew nacham (H5162) — to comfort, to console; the stated purpose of the friends' visit.

Hebrew nekonah — that which is right; ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right (Job 42:7).

Usage

"“Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him”."

"“Then answered Zophar the Naamathite, and said”."

"“Ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath” (Job 42:7)."
